gloss: build, build up; son, daughter: the children who build a house
summary: בָּנָה is to build: an altar, a house, a city, Yahweh’s temple, and to build again what lies in ruins (Gen 8:20; 1Ki 6:1; Amo 9:11); since a house is also a family, to build a man’s house is to raise up his children (Deu 25:9; Rut 4:11), and to “be built” (niphal) is to gain children (Gen 16:2; 30:3). בֵּן, son, and בַּת, daughter, are those children: a son or descendant, the young of an animal, and by a Hebrew idiom anyone belonging to a people, a kind, an age or a fate (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, Num 10:28; בֶּן־שָׁנָה “a year old”, Lev 23:12); Aramaic has בַּר, plural בְּנֵי. Yahweh joins the two words in his promise to David, “Yahweh will make you a house … he shall build a house for my name … I will be to him a father and he shall be to me a son” (2Sa 7:11–14), which Hebrews applies to Jesus (Heb 1:5). Every branch of the Semitic languages has both b‑n‑y “build” and bn “son”, bnt “daughter”, and Arabic files ibn “son” under banā “build”; that scripture joins them is plain, but no text shows “son” being formed from “build”.

words.gloss: son; child, descendant; young of an animal; one belonging to a kind, an age or a fate
words.summary: About 5,000 times, the commonest noun of the root. BDB files בֵּן under no verb; it is kept here because scripture uses the house a man’s sons build (Deu 25:9; Rut 4:11; 2Sa 7:11–14) and every Semitic language pairs bn “son” with b‑n‑y “build”, though no text derives the one from the other.

evidence.note: “What, בְּרִי? and what, בַּר־בִּטְנִי, son of my womb? and what, בַּר־נְדָרָי, son of my vows?”
נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר, kiss the son, lest he be angry; after “You are my son (בְּנִי)” in v. 7.

words.summary: Once, beside בִּנְיָן in the same vision (Ezk 41:13); a single use, its sense fixed by its context and its sibling.

senses.definition: A built structure, measured with the house and the separate place.

evidence.note: He measured the house, a hundred cubits long, and the separate place וְהַבִּנְיָה and its walls, a hundred cubits.

words.summary: Once (Ezk 40:2): what Ezekiel saw on the very high mountain was “as the frame of a city”.

senses.definition: The built frame of a city, seen in vision.

evidence.note: On a very high mountain, וְעָלָיו כְּמִבְנֵה־עִיר, on it as the frame of a city, on the south.
In whom all the building (οἰκοδομή), fitly framed together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
“You are God’s building.”

words.summary: Once in scripture’s Aramaic (Ezr 5:4), of the house of God being rebuilt.

evidence.note: “What are the names of the men who are building דְנָה בִנְיָנָא, this building?”

senses.definition: To build a house or temple, and of Jesus building his ecclesia and raising again the tabernacle of David.

cognates.gloss: build, frame, construct; a building; form of a building, bodily constitution; builder
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give banā “he built it; framed it; constructed it” (of a house or tent), bināʾ and bunyān “a building, a structure”, binya “a form, mode or manner of building; natural constitution”, bannāʾ “a builder”. These answer to the verb and to בִּנְיָן, בִּנְיָה, מִבְנֶה, and binya “form” to תַּבְנִית.

Lane files ibn “a son; a son’s son; a descendant more remote” under the root of banā “build”, and records the Arab philologist ar‑Rāghib’s explanation that the son is so called “because he is the father’s building, made to be so by God”; some held it to be originally banaw. ibn also forms phrases of the Hebrew kind: ibn as‑sabīl “son of the road”, a traveller.
The feminine of ibn, plural banāt, filed in the same article.

cognates.gloss: build, create, form, engender; builder, creator, begetter
cognates.note: The Akkadian verb covers building, a god’s creating, and engendering, and its noun bānû is builder, creator and begetter: the same span as בָּנָה from the house built to the woman built from the rib (Gen 2:22) and the family built (Gen 16:2).

armep x000036390, bānû [creator] N (begetter, builder, creator)

cognates.note: A noun of banû meaning what is made and its form or appearance, as תַּבְנִית is both the pattern built by and the form of a thing.

evidence.locator: armep x000036400, binûtu [creation] N (appearance, creation, creature, form, nature, product)

cognates.note: Rare (Neo-Assyrian and later; Akkadian’s usual word is māru), but the same word as בֵּן.
Segert glosses bnwt “engendering power, virility”, beside the verb b‑n‑y “to build”, as Akkadian banû is both.
Segert vocalizes /bun‑/ and gives bnš “man” as bn “son” + nš “mankind”, the counterpart of בֶּן־אָדָם and Aramaic בַּר אֱנָשׁ.

doctrine.statement: David wanted to build Yahweh a house; Yahweh answered that he would make David a house, raise up his seed after him, and “he shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2Sa 7:5, 11–14, 16), and David took it as “I will build you a house” (2Sa 7:27). Building a house means both a building and a line of sons (Deu 25:9; Rut 4:11). Zechariah says of the man whose name is the Branch, “he shall build the temple of Yahweh … and shall be a priest upon his throne” (Zec 6:12–13), and Amos that Yahweh will build again the fallen tabernacle of David (Amo 9:11). Hebrews applies “I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son” to Jesus (Heb 1:5), Gabriel promises him “the throne of his father David” for ever (Luk 1:32–33), James reads Amos of the gathering of the nations (Act 15:14–16), and Jesus says “I will build my ecclesia” (Mat 16:18), a house of living stones (1Pe 2:5) “whose house are we” (Heb 3:6). From the verses: the son of David who builds Yahweh’s house is Jesus; the house he builds is a people, and the throne promised with it is David’s throne, established for ever.

A בֵּן is one born of his father: Seth, Isaac (Gen 4:25; 21:3). Yahweh calls Israel “my son, my firstborn” (Exo 4:22), and of David’s seed says “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2Sa 7:14). To the king in Zion he says, “You are my son; today I have begotten you” (Psa 2:7): the sonship rests on begetting, and it has a day. Paul reads that day as God raising up Jesus (Act 13:33); Gabriel says the holy one born of Mary “shall be called the Son of God” because the holy spirit would come on her and the power of the Highest overshadow her (Luk 1:35); and Paul writes of God’s Son “born of the seed of David according to the flesh, declared to be the Son of God with power … by the resurrection of the dead” (Rom 1:3–4). From the verses: Jesus is Son of God as the Hebrew word means a son, one begotten, who had his beginning when God begot him of Mary, a son of David by his mother and declared Son with power at his resurrection.

בֶּן־אָדָם is a human being set against God: “God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent” (Num 23:19); “Do not trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation” (Psa 146:3); and Yahweh addresses the prophet as “son of man” (Ezk 2:1). Psalm 8 asks what the son of man is, that God should visit him, and crowns him with glory over the works of God’s hands (Psa 8:5–7); Hebrews says we see this in Jesus, who “partook of flesh and blood” and was made like his brothers in all things (Heb 2:6–9, 14, 17). Psalm 80 asks Yahweh’s hand to be on “the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you made strong for yourself” (Psa 80:18). Daniel sees one like a son of man (כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ) come with the clouds to the Ancient of days and receive the kingdom (Dan 7:13–14), and Jesus says the high priest will see the Son of man at the right hand of power, coming on the clouds (Mat 26:64). From the verses: the title Jesus takes for himself names him a man of our nature, mortal in himself, whom God made strong, set at his right hand and will give the kingdom.

Scripture calls those who belong to Yahweh his sons: “You are sons to Yahweh your God” (Deu 14:1), “sons of the living God” (Hos 2:1; Rom 9:26), and Luke calls Adam “the son of God” (Luk 3:38). In Gen 4:26, in Enosh’s day, men began to call on the name of Yahweh. In Gen 6 “the sons of God saw the daughters of man … and took them wives of all whom they chose” (Gen 6:2), and Yahweh’s judgment that follows is on man, “for he is flesh” (Gen 6:3). Jesus says the angels of God in heaven neither marry nor are given in marriage (Mat 22:30). From the verses: the sons of God of Gen 6 were men, the line that called on Yahweh’s name, who married outside it.

“The stone which the builders (הַבּוֹנִים) rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing” (Psa 118:22–23). Jesus quotes it to the chief priests and Pharisees, who “perceived that he spoke of them” (Mat 21:42–45); Peter says it to the rulers, elders and scribes: “This is the stone which was set at nought by you builders” (Act 4:11); and those who come to him are built up as living stones into a spiritual house (1Pe 2:4–7). From the verses: the builders were Israel’s rulers, who rejected Jesus; Yahweh raised him to be the head stone, and builds his house on him.

Moses was to make the tabernacle and its vessels by the תַּבְנִית Yahweh showed him on the mount (Exo 25:9, 40), and David gave Solomon the תַּבְנִית of the temple “in writing from the hand of Yahweh” (1Ch 28:11, 19). Hebrews quotes Exo 25:40 to say that the priests “serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things”, and that it was necessary for the copies of the things in the heavens to be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices; Christ entered not a holy place made with hands, the figure of the true, but heaven itself (Heb 8:5; 9:23–24). From the verses: the tabernacle was built to a pattern that pointed beyond itself, to Christ’s entry into the presence of God.

note: The corpus keys the verb בנה (BDB b.cb.aa), and BDB files בֵּן (b.ca.aa) and בַּת (b.ca.at) under no root; they are kept here on scripture’s joining of son and house and on the cognates, which pair bn and bny in every branch (Anderson–Moser list them as separate roots SEM000015–17). Aramaic בַּר (xb.al.ab) is taken as the same word as בֵּן because its plural is built on bn (בְּנֵי, בְּנוֹהִי); Hebrew בַּר (b.cv.ac, Psa 2:12; Pro 31:2) likewise. Key counts are inflated by spelling: xb.al.ab is double-filed on about 1,800 Hebrew בְּנֵי tokens, b.cv.ac on בַּר “grain” (Amo 5:11; 8:6; Psa 72:16) and בְּרִי “moisture” (Job 37:11), b.cb.aa takes about 90 tokens of בְּנוֹת “daughters of” and בָּנוּ “us”, and b.ca.at takes infinitives לִבְנוֹת (Jer 1:10 is cited under the verb). Psa 2:12 נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר is read “kiss the son” from v. 7; the Septuagint has δράξασθε παιδείας and gives no Greek bridge. The Peshitta words are not keyed in BDB. Proper names of the root have no entries yet: Benaiah (b.cb.ag), Bani (b.cb.ad), Binnui (b.cb.ac), Bunni (b.cb.ae), Ibneiah and Ibnijah (b.cb.ak, b.cb.al), Mebunnai (b.cb.an), Ben-oni (b.ca.ad), Ben-hadad, Ben-ammi and the other בֶּן־ names (b.ca.ab–b.ca.as); Jabneel and Jabneh (b.cb.ai, b.cb.aj) are places. Benjamin is in names/benjamin.json. γέεννα, which Thayer derives through בְּנֵי הִנֹּם, is a loan of גֵּי הִנֹּם and belongs with גיא. The Gen 6 doctrine item and the reading of Psa 82:6 as Israel’s judges are judgment calls for review. Ge’ez has no bn “son” (it uses wald) and is not cited.
